title: Arithmetic Operators
description: The five arithmetic operators, what the remainder is for, and the order Java works in.

content.value: Java has five arithmetic operators. `+` adds, `-` subtracts, `*` multiplies, `/` divides, and `%` gives the **remainder** after a division.

content.caption: 17 divided by 5 is 3 with 2 left over: `/` gives the 3, `%` gives the 2.

content.text: Each friend gets 3 sweets: that is `/`. The 2 sweets nobody gets are left over: that is `%`.

items.title: Both int
items.text: Two `int` values give an `int`. The .4 is thrown away.

items.title: One double
items.text: Make one side a `double` when you want the decimal answer.

content.question: What does `System.out.println(7 / 2);` print?
content.explain: Both are `int`, so the answer is a whole number: 2 goes into 7 three times. The 1 left over is what `7 % 2` gives.

items.sub: `n % 2` is 0 for even numbers, 1 for odd ones.
If `a % b` is 0, b fits into a with nothing left.

steps.note: A total number of seconds to split into units.
3600 seconds make an hour. 3725 / 3600 is 1 whole hour.
`3725 % 3600` is 125, the part that was not a whole hour. 125 / 60 is 2 whole minutes.
`3725 % 60` is what is left after whole minutes: 5.
Join it all into one line.

content.title: Splitting seconds into units
content.outro: The pattern: divide for the big unit, take the remainder, repeat. It also turns paise into rupees.

content.question: What does `System.out.println(29 % 10);` print?
content.explain: 10 goes into 29 twice with 9 left over, and `%` gives the left over part.

content.value: Java follows maths: `*`, `/` and `%` happen before `+` and `-`. Equal rank goes left to right. Round brackets beat everything.

content.caption: Tip: once a sum has more than two operators, add brackets even where Java does not need them. `price + (price * TAX_RATE)` says what you meant.

content.question: What does `System.out.println(10 - 4 - 3);` print?
content.explain: Equal rank goes left to right: `(10 - 4) - 3` is 3. Right to left would give 9, a bug that is hard to see.

content.caption: Sample run: type `900` then `4` and it prints `Each person pays 225.0`. `total` is a `double`, so the division keeps decimals. Two `int` values would need a cast, as in Module 2.

items.title: int: crash
items.text: Stops the program with an `ArithmeticException: / by zero`.

items.title: double: odd values
items.text: No crash, but `NaN` means "not a number". Neither is useful.

content.value: So a program that divides by a typed number should check it first. That check is a decision, and decisions are the next module.

practice.question: Store 47 in an `int`. Print whether it is even by printing `47 % 2`, then print its last digit.
Ask for a number of minutes, then print how many whole hours and how many minutes are left over.
Work out `2 + 3 * 4 - 6 / 2` in your head first, then print it and check whether you were right.

quiz.question: What does `17 % 5` give?
options: 3, the whole part of the division
quiz.explain: 5 goes into 17 three times with 2 left over. `/` gives the 3 and `%` gives the 2.

quiz.question: How do you test whether an `int` called `n` is even?
quiz.explain: An even number divides by 2 with nothing left over, so its remainder is 0. Odd numbers give 1.

quiz.question: What does `System.out.println(2 + 3 * 4);` print?
quiz.explain: Multiplication happens before addition, so `3 * 4` is worked out first. Brackets round `2 + 3` would give 20.

quiz.question: What does `10 - 4 - 3` give, and why?
options: 3, because equal ranking operators go left to right
9, because the right hand pair goes first
It is ambiguous, so Java reports an error
quiz.explain: Both operators rank the same, so Java works left to right: `(10 - 4) - 3`, which is 3.

quiz.question: Given `int totalSeconds = 3725;`, what does `totalSeconds % 60` give?
options: 5, the seconds left after taking whole minutes
125, the seconds left after taking whole hours
quiz.explain: `% 60` is what remains once every whole minute has been removed, which is the seconds part of the time.

quiz.question: What happens when you run `System.out.println(5 / 0);`?
options: The program stops with an ArithmeticException.
quiz.explain: Whole-number division by zero has no answer, so Java throws an ArithmeticException. `5.0 / 0` is different: doubles give `Infinity`.
